newsitem.title: USA: Sharp increase in U.S. soybean acreage seen.
newsitem.headline: Sharp increase in U.S. soybean acreage seen.

text.p: High soybean prices will likely spur a sizable increase in 1997 U.S. soybean acreage on the U.S. Department of Agriculture's next planting intentions report, oilseed analysts said.

Soybean acreage estimates in the March 31 USDA report ranged from 65.5 million to 67 million acres, analysts and those who attended the annual meeting of the National Institute of Oilseed Products said Wednesday.
"A lot of farmers are looking at old crop cash prices instead of spreads," said Richard Loewy, analyst with AgResources Co. in Chicago.
The corn to soybean cash price ratio at the time farmers were surveyed on planting intentions by the USDA was more favorable to soybeans, which will result in higher soybean acreage, Loewy said.
In its latest supply and demand forecast, the USDA put 1996/97 soybean acreage at 64.2 million acres.
Another analyst said, with the U.S. moving away from subsidised agriculture, farmers would make their 1997 planting decisions based on what brings the biggest profits.
"This year, farmers are looking at a record net return on soybeans versus corn," she said.
She forecast soybean acreage to climb as high as 67 million acres.

Another analyst cautioned that although the United States could end up with soybean acreage exceeding 66 million acres, the USDA might not put out such a high forecast in their first acreage report of the year.
"History shows us that they (USDA) might not put it (high acreage) in the first report," said Mickey Luth, analyst with the Laifa Group in Chicago.
Many analysts and others attending the meeting also expect the pace of U.S. soybean exports to drop sharply in the next six months as crops from South America hit export channels.
The USDA had forecast 1996/97 US soybean exports at 900 million bushels, but that figure could easily drop to 875 to 880 million bushels, analysts told the group.
The high cost of U.S. soybeans relative to those from South America is likely to sway customers that typically only buy from the United States, one analyst said.
"Taiwan last year imported almost 100 percent of its beans from the U.S., but this week they decided that the $7.00 (per bushel) discount was enough to make them buy Brazilian," the analyst said.
